name: Mining

summary: Autonomous haulage and ore-body modelling are the established deployments in a sector that adopted automation early. Mining AI splits into two horizons: exploration - long-term forecasting from satellite, magnetic, and core-scan data toward drilling targets - and site operations, where sensor streams and telemetry drive machinery, maintenance, and safety minute by minute.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 7.2 percent of firms in mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction reported using AI in the most recent period, down slightly from 7.9 percent in the prior period. That measured figure, drawn directly from firms rather than estimated, makes mining one of the better-documented sectors for adoption, even if the share remains modest in absolute terms. The small decline between periods suggests that uptake is not yet on a steady upward trajectory across the broad sector, though it masks considerable variation between large, technically sophisticated operators and smaller firms.

Where AI is deployed, the applications cluster around two distinct problems: finding ore bodies and operating equipment once a deposit is in production. On the exploration side, KoBold Metals represents the clearest AI-native bet in the sector, applying machine learning and geospatial modelling to target battery-metal deposits including lithium, cobalt, copper, and nickel, with its Mingomba project in Zambia positioned to become one of the world's largest copper mines. GeologicAI approaches the same problem from a different angle, combining RGB, XRF, hyperspectral, and LiDAR sensors in multi-sensor core scanning systems used by operators including Agnico Eagle, and describing its offering as the only platform combining high-fidelity data, robust analytics, and domain expertise across the full mining cycle.

On the operational side, the autonomous equipment layer is documented most directly by Komatsu, one of the two dominant mining-equipment makers, which has entered a strategic partnership with AIM Intelligent Machines for autonomous operation of bulldozers and hydraulic excavators and publishes its autonomous haulage and fleet-management technology as a commercial product line. Rio Tinto's automation program, running autonomous haul trucks and drills at scale, is the sector's primary-source record of what day-to-day operational AI looks like in production mining. Freeport-McMoRan applies machine learning to mill processing, targeting throughput and ore recovery at existing copper operations rather than exploration. Newmont, among the major gold miners, uses AI for drill-core analysis, predictive maintenance, and automated safety monitoring.

The public data infrastructure underpinning much of this work sits with the USGS Mineral Resources Program, which serves as the nation's authoritative source of mineral resource information and whose satellite, geophysical, and historical datasets provide the training material for exploration models. The USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, known as Earth MRI, is systematically re-mapping US geology with modern geophysics, delivering the high-quality subsurface data that machine-learning prospectivity work on critical minerals depends on. High-resolution airborne radiometric surveys are covering more ground than ever, per Earth MRI, extending the dataset available to computational exploration methods.

The policy and standards environment is shaped by two organizations whose pages do not report specific AI metrics but define the terrain operators navigate. The National Mining Association, as the only national trade organization serving as the voice of US mining before Congress and federal agencies, tracks regulatory change affecting technology adoption across American operations. The International Council on Mining and Metals, whose 2025 safety report covers fatalities, injuries, and workplace hazards across its member companies, frames automation and digital transformation within a broader ESG and safety accountability structure, and its members include operators running some of the most advanced autonomous systems in the industry.

A reader weighing deployment should take from this evidence that AI in mining is genuinely operating at scale in specific, bounded applications, particularly autonomous haulage, core scanning, mill optimization, and predictive maintenance, rather than as a generalized enterprise capability. The vendor ecosystem is split between large equipment manufacturers embedding autonomy into machinery and specialist software firms processing geological data. The public data layer from USGS and Earth MRI lowers the cost of entry for exploration-side machine learning. The measured adoption rate, while not high in absolute terms, reflects a capital-intensive sector where a single application proving ROI at one large operation can justify substantial investment, and where the Society for Mining, Metallurgy and Exploration continues to publish the technical research base that informs those decisions.
